bio.en: April Dunford is the author of "Obviously Awesome" and one of the world's leading product-positioning experts, with 25 years as a B2B VP of marketing and 200+ tech companies advised (including Epic Games and Google); she turned her five-step positioning method — competitive alternatives, differentiated capabilities, value themes, best-fit customers, market category — into a book that helps founders, PMs, and GTM teams turn positioning from a fuzzy concept into an executable sales story.
bio.zh: April Dunford 是《Obviously Awesome》的作者、全球最权威的产品定位专家之一，拥有 25 年 B2B 营销 VP 经验，合作过 200 多家科技公司（含 Epic Games、Google 等）；她把自己的「五步定位法」（竞争替代方案→差异化能力→价值主题→最佳契合客户→市场品类）写成书，帮助创始人、PM 和 GTM 团队把「定位」从模糊的概念变成可执行的销售故事。

summary.en: April Dunford defines positioning as "how your product is best in the world at delivering value a well-defined set of customers cares about" and lays out an actionable five-step method: figure out what you must beat (status quo plus shortlist), list differentiated capabilities, translate them into value themes, define your best-fit customers, then pick the market category that makes that value obvious. She stresses positioning is a team sport — marketing, product, sales, and the CEO must align or everyone tells a different story — and the output is not just a doc but a testable sales narrative. Weak-positioning signals include customers saying "say that again" or "I can do that in a spreadsheet" on sales calls. She also clears up common confusions: positioning is the upstream input to messaging and branding; early products should keep a loose "positioning thesis" and let the market pull them toward the real fit (like a net cast wide, then tightened); and in a B2B purchase with 5–7 people involved, the only persona that matters is the "champion" in the account, whom all marketing should first arm.
summary.zh: April Dunford 把定位定义为「你的产品如何最好地交付某组客户非常在乎的价值」，并给出一个可执行的五步法：先想清楚你要打败什么（现状+短名单），再列差异化能力、翻译成价值主题、定义最佳契合客户、最后选让价值 obvious 的市场品类。她强调定位是团队运动——市场、产品、销售、CEO 必须一起达成一致，否则各说各话；输出不只是一份文档，而是一个能测试的销售叙事。弱定位的信号包括客户在销售电话里说「再说一遍」或「我用表格就能做」。她还厘清了几个常见混淆：定位是 messaging 和品牌的上游输入；早期产品应保持「定位假设」松一点、让市场把你拉向真正契合的细分（像渔网先撒宽、再收紧）；在 B2B 购买里 5–7 人参与，但唯一关键的人物画像是「账户里的 champion（推手）」，所有营销都应先武装他。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right, let's do it. So for listeners who maybe aren't super familiar with your background and how you came to be such an expert on positioning, could you just briefly share your journey to what you do today?
turns.zh: 好，来吧。对可能不太熟悉你背景、以及你怎么成了定位专家的听众，能简单分享一下你走到今天这条路吗？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Yeah, sure. So my background is I didn't study marketing in school, I studied engineering. Straight out of engineering school, I got a job, a product marketing job at a startup. And I've been doing this a long time, so this was back when startups weren't even cool and we just called them small companies.
turns.zh: 行。我的背景是，我在学校没学营销，学的是工程。工程一毕业，我拿了个小创业公司的一个工作——产品营销的活。我做这个很久了，那是创业公司还不酷、我们就叫它们小公司的时候。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So I got a job at a little company and then that company, I was assigned to a product that was kind of a loser and we weren't selling very much. We ended up repositioning it and the thing took off, it got hugely successful. That company got acquired, my boss quit and they made me the vice president of marketing. I still have no idea why. And then I decided, well, this is my jam, this is what I do now.
turns.zh: 我在家小公司，被分配到一个有点失败的产品，卖得不太好。我们最后给它重新定位，那东西起飞了，大获成功。公司被收购，我老板走了，他们让我当了营销 VP。我到现在都不知道为啥。然后我决定，行，这就是我的菜，我现在就干这个。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And in particular, we had a handful of products there, the positioning also seemed kind of weak. And so I embarked on this journey of, hey, positioning seems to be really important because when we get it wrong, everything sucks, and when we get it right, we all make all kinds of money, so I should figure out how to do this properly.
turns.zh: 特别的是，我们那有一堆产品，定位也显得有点弱。于是我踏上一段旅程——定位好像非常重要，因为当我们搞错时，一切都烂；当我们搞对时，大家都赚大钱，所以我该搞明白怎么正确地做这个。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so I read a bunch of books, took a bunch of courses and what I discovered is that positioning is this foundational marketing concept, but we didn't really have a methodology for doing it. And so from that point forward, I became a repeat vice president of marketing at a series of startups. So I think I did seven and six of those got acquired.
turns.zh: 所以我读了一堆书、上了一堆课，发现定位是个基础的营销概念，但我们其实没有做它的方法论。从那以后，我成了多家创业公司的「复读」营销 VP。我想我做了七家，其中六家被收购。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So I repositioned a lot of products across that and positioning became my specialty. Basically, if you were looking for a vice president of marketing and I came into the interview, the reason you hired me is because your positioning was crappy and I could talk intelligently about how we were going to fix that.
turns.zh: 所以我在那之间重新定位了很多产品，定位成了我的专长。基本上，如果你在找营销 VP、我进来面试，你雇我的原因是你的定位很烂，而我能聪明地聊我们要怎么修。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And then about five, six years ago, I decided I wanted to go do something different and so I made the switch to consulting and now that's all I do. So I basically do positioning. Even more specifically though, I really focused on, I only do tech companies. I only do B2B companies, because my background is all really B2B and I don't really get consumer.
turns.zh: 大约五六年前，我想做点不一样的，就转去做咨询，现在只做这个。所以我基本就做定位。更具体地说，我只做科技公司、只做 B2B 公司，因为我的背景全是 B2B，我不太懂消费者。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And mainly I work with startups. For the most part it's what I would call a growth stage startup, post series A, series B, but occasionally I do some really, really big companies that have weird positioning stuff going on, like they've acquired a bunch of things and they're trying to turn it into a business unit or something and there's no story around that. So that's how I got here.
turns.zh: 而且我主要跟创业公司合作。大多数时候是我叫「增长期创业公司」——A 轮后、B 轮——但偶尔我也做真正的大公司，它们有奇怪的定位问题，比如收购了一堆东西、想把它变成一个业务单元、但周围没故事。所以我是这么走到这的。

turns.zh: 太棒了。铺垫一下，你到现在大概跟多少家公司合作过、帮它们做定位？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: It's around 200-

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: ... I think. I think, I suspect that I have done more positioning than anybody on the planet.
turns.zh: ——我想是。我怀疑我做的定位比地球上任何人都多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was just going to say that.
turns.zh: 我正想说这个。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: That's my suspicion. I certainly have positioned more B2B tech companies than anybody. I don't know how anybody's going to get me on that one.
turns.zh: 那是我的怀疑。我定位过的 B2B 科技公司肯定比任何人都多。我不知道谁能在这点上超过我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I would not be surprised. Okay, so I'm excited to learn a lot from our conversation along those lines. I'm curious, what's the most interesting or unusual company that you've worked with around positioning and what happened there?
turns.zh: 我不会惊讶。好，我超兴奋能从这角度学很多。我好奇，你合作过的最有趣或最不寻常的公司是哪个，那发生了什么？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: The fun part about positioning is that when you do this kind of work, you get to dive into a market that maybe you haven't thought very much about. So it's like, I'm going to drop some names, but this week I'm working with Epic Games on a product that they have called Twinmotion, which is absolutely mind-blowing tech. You should look at it.
turns.zh: 定位好玩的地方是，做这种工作时，你会扎进一个你可能没怎么想过的市场。所以我丢几个名字，这周我在跟 Epic Games 做一个叫 Twinmotion 的产品，那技术绝对让人 mind-blowing。你应该看看。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: I don't come from that world of doing three dimensional graphic stuff, and so it's fun to just do a big, deep dive on that and look at everything in the space and look at what's possible and what isn't possible there.
turns.zh: 我不是做三维图形那行的，所以有趣的是深挖那个、看那领域里的一切、看什么可能、什么不可能。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so I've done everything from stuff like that to I come from databases. And so I have a lot of companies doing deep data stuff and data analytics stuff, which I find really interesting and cool, but then occasionally you'll get one that makes you think about your life differently.
turns.zh: 所以我做过从那种到——我来自数据库。所以我有好多公司做深度数据、数据分析的东西，我觉得很有趣很酷，但偶尔你会遇到一个让你重新想自己生活的。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: I did one a year or so ago and the company's called Bluelight Analytics. And what they do is technology for helping certain kinds of dentistry instruments work better. And so I didn't really think much about what happens in the dentist office until I went to do this workshop.
turns.zh: 一年多前我做了一个，公司叫 Bluelight Analytics。他们做的是帮某些牙科器械更好工作的技术。所以在去做那个工作坊前，我没真想过牙医办公室里发生啥。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And then we spent the whole time talking about it's terrifying actually, half the stuff that a dentist does in your mouth is very likely to fail because the equipment is terrible and the way they actually do things like cure fillings is actually really terrible. And so sometimes I learn things in these workshops that I wish I didn't know. I'm a little bit scared going to the dentist now.
turns.zh: 然后我们整个时间都在聊——其实挺吓人的——牙医在你嘴里做的有一半极可能失败，因为设备很糟、他们固化补牙之类的方式真的很糟。所以有时我在这些工作坊里学到我不希望知道的事。我现在去看牙医有点怕。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man, sounds like they-
turns.zh: 哦老天，听起来他们——

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Sorry to the Bluelight guys, but yeah.
turns.zh: 对 Bluelight 那帮人抱歉，但是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I thought Bluelight was going to be like not getting exposed to blue light when you're trying to get asleep.
turns.zh: 我本来以为 Bluelight 是「睡觉前别被蓝光照射」那种。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: No. No. I wish. That would make me not make me so scared of the dentist.
turns.zh: 不。不。我倒希望是。那会让我没那么怕牙医。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Also a problem. How do you know that you have a positioning problem and that you should focus on positioning?
turns.zh: 也是个问题。你怎么知道你有定位问题、该聚焦定位？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So this is a thing that people ask me this a lot. And I think what people want, and I want this too, what I wish we had was a metric that I could say, "Hey, when you start seeing this metric go in this direction, then you know the positioning is bad." But unfortunately, weak positioning gets you all the way across the pipeline.
turns.zh: 这是人们常问我的。我觉得人们想要的、我也想要的，是一个指标，能说「嘿，当你看到这指标往这方向走，你就知道定位烂了」。但不幸的是，弱定位会一路坑你到管道尽头。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Weak positioning hurts you in the early stages of pipeline in that people don't really get what you are, so they're not responding to your marketing the way they should. And you'll get this sluggishness in the middle of your pipeline, particularly if you have sales people. The light doesn't come on until they've had three calls with the sales rep and then the light comes on.
turns.zh: 弱定位在管道早期伤害你——人们不真懂你是啥，所以不像他们该有的那样回应你的营销。管道中间你会感到 sluggish，尤其如果你有销售。灯要到他们跟销售代表打了三个电话才亮。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And then sometimes what you'll get is your sales team is actually really good at selling the stuff, but the positioning's wrong, so you close a lot of deals, but then people get using the product and they're like, "Wait a minute, this isn't the thing that I thought it was or it doesn't do what I expected it to do," and then they churn out on you.
turns.zh: 然后有时你的情况是销售团队其实很会卖，但定位错了，所以你关了很多单，但人们用上产品后「等等，这不是我以为的东西、或它没做我以为它能做的」，然后他们 churn 掉。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So all your metrics look bad and you can only tell they look bad by comparing them to your own metrics. And so it's really hard to measure if the positioning isn't working or not.
turns.zh: 所以你所有指标都难看，而你只能通过跟你自己的指标比，才知道它们难看。所以真的很难衡量定位是不是没工作。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Back when I used to be VP marketing, what I would do to assess this is I'd be the brand new VP of marketing, I'd come on board and I'd say, "Well, I'm just going to go hang out with sales for a bit." And you can really hear it in sales calls, particularly in an initial sales call with a client.
turns.zh: 我当营销 VP 时，评估这个的做法是——我刚当上新营销 VP，我会说「好，我去销售那待一会」。你在销售电话里真能听到，尤其初次销售电话。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And what you'll hear is things like the customer comes on, your sales rep comes on, and your sales rep's doing a great job pitching the product like, "Oh, we got this thing and it does this, that, and the other thing."
turns.zh: 你会听到：客户上来，你的销售代表上来，销售代表超会 pitch 产品「哦我们有这东西，它做这个、那个、还有那个」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And they'll get a certain way through the pitch and you can see the customer's just like, "Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Just back it up and pitch it to me again." That's probably the most common one I get is, "Huh? Could you just say that again? Could you just back up to the beginning and do that thing from the beginning?"
turns.zh: 他们会 pitch 到某个程度，你能看到客户就「对对对。倒回去再给我 pitch 一遍」。我最常听到的可能就是这个：「嗯？你能再说一遍吗？能倒回开头从那开始吗？」

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So there's this confusion. Sometimes what you'll get is the even worse one is the customer thinks they know exactly what you are, but you ain't that. So you'll get people who say, "Yeah. Yeah. I get it, you're just like Salesforce." And you're like, "Oh actually, no, we're nothing like Salesforce. Sorry. No, that's it. Let me back up and start from the beginning."
turns.zh: 所以有这种困惑。有时更糟的是客户以为他们 exact 知道你是啥，但你不是那个。你会遇到人说「对对，我懂，你就像 Salesforce」。你说「哦其实不，我们跟 Salesforce 完全不同。抱歉。对，就那样。让我倒回去从头开始」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Or you'll get this and this one is actually terrible where people will say, "Well, I get it. I mean, I totally get it. I totally get what you do. I just don't get why anyone would pay for that. I can do that in a spreadsheet. I don't get it." So they think they get what you do, but they don't really understand the value.
turns.zh: 或者你会遇到这个——其实挺糟的——人们说「嗯我懂。我完全懂。我完全懂你做啥。我只是不懂为什么有人会为那个付钱。我用电子表格就能做。我不懂」。所以他们以为懂你做啥，但没真懂价值。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so if you start hearing stuff like that in an initial sales call, those are usually good signs that the positioning is weak.
turns.zh: 所以如果你在初次销售电话里开始听到这类话，通常就是定位弱的好信号。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really helpful. Backing up a little bit, we jumped right in. I'm curious how you even describe positioning, what the heck is positioning? And broadly, just why is it important for people to think about?
turns.zh: 那真有帮助。回退一点，我们直接跳进来了。我好奇你怎么描述定位，定位到底是啥？ broadly，为什么人们该想这个？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: In my opinion, it's really misunderstood, which is funny because it's not a new concept. We've been talking about positioning since the '80s, but like a lot of things in marketing people have stretched the definition or there's different definitions, even among marketing people. If I had a dozen vice presidents of marketing together in a room and said, "Hey, define positioning," we'd get a dozen different definitions.
turns.zh: 我觉得它被严重误解，好笑的是它不是新概念。我们从 80 年代就在聊定位，但像营销里很多东西，人们把定义拉伸了，或即便在营销人里也有不同定义。如果我把一打营销 VP 放一屋问「嘿，定义定位」，我会得到一打不同定义。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: But I think about it this way, positioning defines how your product is the best in the world, delivering some value that a well-defined set of companies care a lot about. So put another way, it encompasses a lot of things, it defines what are the alternatives to what you do? How are you different? What value can you deliver that no other product on the market can?
turns.zh: 但我是这么想的：定位定义你的产品怎么在世界上最好地交付某种价值——一组定义明确的公司非常在乎的那种价值。换种说法，它涵盖很多：它定义你做的东西的替代方案是啥？你哪不同？你能交付市场上其他产品都交付不了的价值是啥？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And oh, by the way, who cares a lot about that value? So who is it that you're trying to target? And then it also encompasses the definition of your market category or what market is it that you intend to win.
turns.zh: 还有，顺带，谁非常在乎那个价值？所以你要打的目标是谁？然后它也涵盖你的市场品类的定义——你打算赢的是哪个市场？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such a succinct, simple way of thinking about it. Something that I've been thinking about is this isn't something just founders should care about. PMs on teams that are building a product should think about this, leaders, GMs of business units. This applies across the board, basically to any product, whether it's the entire company or just one feature.
turns.zh: 那是想这件事超简洁、超简单的方式。我一直在想的是，这不只创始人该在乎。建产品的 PM、领导者、业务单元 GM 都该想这个。这全方位适用，基本上对任何产品——无论是整个公司还是一个功能。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Well, this is one of the things that where I think people get into weak positioning. One of the things that happens in companies, and I see this a lot where the founder has an idea what the positioning is, but then you go to the marketing department and it's a little bit different, not a lot different, but a little bit different.
turns.zh: 嗯，这正是我觉得人们陷入弱定位的一点。公司里发生的事——我常看到——创始人心里有个定位是啥的想法，但你走到市场部，有点不同，不是大不同，是小不同。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And then you sit in on the sales pitch and that's a little bit different again. And then you walk over to the product team and they're thinking about it slightly differently. So I think a lot of weak positioning comes from the fact that we don't have perfect alignment across the team on all these piece parts of positioning.
turns.zh: 然后你旁听销售 pitch，又有点不同。然后你走到产品团队，他们想得又稍不同。所以我觉得很多弱定位来自：我们对定位的所有零件没有完美的跨团队对齐。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So in the work I do, and even back when I was a VP marketing, if we're going to fix this thing, we can't just have the marketing department or just the product managers sit down and cook up new positioning and then heave it over the wall to everybody else, it actually needs to be a group effort. It's a team sport.
turns.zh: 所以在我的工作里、甚至我当营销 VP 时，如果要修这个，我们不能只让市场部或只让 PM 坐下来炮制新定位然后扔过墙给别人，它其实得是 group effort。是团队运动。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So if we're going to do positioning well and then actually have that positioning stick and get adopted the way we want it to across the company, if we're going to do a positioning exercise, ideally we've got marketing, product, sales, customer success, and anybody else we need from the executive team, particularly the CEO, together in a room when we're building it.
turns.zh: 所以如果我们想做好定位、然后让那个定位真的粘住、按我们想要的方式被全公司采用，如果我们要做定位 exercise，理想情况下我们有市场、产品、销售、客户成功、以及我们从高管团队需要的任何人——尤其 CEO——一起在屋里建它。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So that we can all bring our expertise to the table, bring our understanding of what customers do and our product to the table, thrash around on it a little bit until we get agreement on it. And then now that we've all got agreement and alignment around it, then we can all go execute on it and we're all singing the same song.
turns.zh: 这样我们都能把专长、对客户做什么的理解、对我们产品的理解带到桌上，稍微折腾一下直到我们对它达成一致。然后既然我们都有了一致和对齐，我们就能都去执行它，我们都在唱同一首歌。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so interesting. How often do you find that the problem is misalignment within the company versus just they don't actually have the right positioning and that's the problem?
turns.zh: 太有意思了。你发现问题是公司内部没对齐，vs 只是他们其实没有对的定位、那才是问题——这两种情况各多常？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Well, a lot of times it's misalignment. I would say the majority of the time it's misalignment, because what it is a piece of the company has it right, but the other pieces don't. So I get one of two things are happening.
turns.zh: 嗯，很多时候是没对齐。我会说大多数时候是没对齐，因为情况是公司某块对了，但其他块不对。所以我看到两种之一在发生。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So sometimes what I'll get is the founder comes to me and the founder says, "I know exactly how to tell this story. You put me in front of a customer, I crush it every time. I know how to position this thing. I know how to do whatever. But we've gotten big now and I got a brand new VP marketing and I got a brand new VP sales and I just hired somebody to do product and they don't understand it the way I understand it."
turns.zh: 有时是创始人来找我，说「我 exact 知道怎么讲这个故事。你把我放客户面前，我每次都 crush 它。我知道怎么定位这东西。我知道怎么做。但我们现在变大了，我招了个全新的营销 VP、全新的销售 VP，我刚招了个人做产品，他们不像我这么理解」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: "And when I listen in on a sales call, what I hear is all wrong, that it's not it. When I look at our marketing, what I see, that's not it. And I've tried to get everybody in alignment and I can't. And so I need you to come in here and facilitate a thing where we can all get in alignment." That happens a lot.
turns.zh: 「我旁听销售电话，听到的全错，那不是它。我看我们的营销，看到的，那不是它。我试过让所有人对齐，但我做不到。所以我需要你进来 facilitate 一个事，让我们都能对齐」。那常发生。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: The other one I get is kind of the opposite of that, where you've got a founder that used to run sales, used to do all the deals, used to do everything, had their arms around this market very tight at one point and then the company's grown, often very quickly. They've hired a bunch of very senior people to run pieces, but at the same time, the market itself has shifted a lot.
turns.zh: 我收到的另一种正好相反：创始人以前跑销售、做所有单子、以前把所有事都揽在怀里、一度把市场抓得超紧，然后公司长大了，常很快。他们招了一堆很资深的人分管各块，但与此同时市场本身变了很多。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so I'll get approached then often by the head of product or the head of marketing that comes in and says, "I don't think we have this right. I think we're actually positioned for what the market used to be. And I'm having a hard time getting the founder, having their heads around it and everybody else on the team, because we're all coming at it with different information."
turns.zh: 于是常是产品或市场头进来跟我说「我觉得我们这不对。我觉得我们其实是为市场过去那样定位的。我很难让创始人、让团队其他人都想通，因为我们都拿着不同的信息」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so sales sees what's happening in sales. Marketing sees what's happening in marketing. The founder's getting pulled into certain deals, but not all the deals. Product's seeing what's happening in the thing. And so again, there's pieces of it there, but we're not all in alignment and agreement. And so we got to get everybody together and then work through it.
turns.zh: 所以销售看销售里发生的，市场看市场里发生的，创始人被拉进某些单子但不是所有，产品看产品里发生的。所以 again，那里有它的碎片，但我们没全对齐、没达成一致。所以我们得把所有人聚一起然后过一遍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What does it look like when you've nailed it, when you are maybe in a good place with positioning? And also just along those-
turns.zh: 当你搞定时、当你在定位上处于好位置时，它长啥样？还有就那些——

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Yeah-

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Go for it. Go for it.
turns.zh: 说吧。说吧。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: ... it's interesting because when it's working really well, it feels like magic and really great positioning feels obvious. You pitch it to people and they're like, "Well, of course that's it. What else could it be?"
turns.zh: ——有意思的是，当它工作得特别好，它像魔法，真正好的定位感觉 obvious。你 pitch 给人们，他们「嗯，当然就是它。还能是别的啥？」

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: One of my favorite companies, this is a company I worked with a little bit a couple of years ago is Postman. You know these folks?
turns.zh: 我最爱的公司之一——这是我几年前稍微合作过的一家——是 Postman。你认识这帮人吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So they basically have an API platform, a platform for building and using APIs. And just how I described that right there is so simple, it's so simple, of course that's what it is. But it was not simple getting there and that's not the way they were always describing themselves. And if you run that back three years ago, that's not at all what you would have gotten as the pitch for Postman.
turns.zh: 他们基本有个 API 平台，建和使用 API 的平台。我刚刚描述它的方式就这么简单，这么简单，当然那就是它。但到那不简单，而且那不是他们一直描述自己的方式。你倒回三年前，那根本不是你会听到的 Postman 的 pitch。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: But really, really great positioning just feels like it's so clear, it's so simple, of course that's what it is, of course, and of course we need one of those. If we're serious about APIs, why would we not have a platform for building and managing APIs? Of course we need that. And so it's hard to judge sometimes from the outside.
turns.zh: 但真正、真正好的定位就感觉这么清晰、这么简单——当然就是它，当然，而且当然我们需要一个。如果我们认真搞 API，我们为啥不该有个建和管理 API 的平台？当然我们需要。所以从外面有时很难判断。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: The other thing is that positioning is somewhat like messaging in some ways in that it's not a static thing, it changes over time. Your product itself doesn't stay the same, the market doesn't stay the same, and so things will shift over time. And so you can have good positioning that suddenly becomes bad positioning and it's not great positioning anymore, or good positioning that goes sideways or whatever, then you got to come back.
turns.zh: 另一件事是，定位在有些方面有点像 messaging，它不是静态的，随时间变。你的产品本身不变？市场不变？所以事会随时间移。所以你可能有好定位突然变坏定位，它不再是好定位了，或好定位走偏了，然后你得回来。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so usually I think there's value in checking in on your positioning because it's really hard. Again, I don't have a measurement to say yes or no, the positioning's working. And so I think there's no harm in checking in on it, going through a process to walk through it and just check in and see, could it be better? Maybe we could tighten this up. Maybe this could be a lot better than it is right now, but we've never sat down and actually deliberately looked at it.
turns.zh: 所以通常我觉得值得 check in 你的定位，因为这真的难。again，我没有个测量说 yes 或 no 定位在起作用。所以我觉得 check in 没坏处，走个流程过一遍、就 check in 看看能不能更好？也许我们能收紧这个。也许这能比现在好很多，但我们从没坐下来真的刻意看过它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to make it even a little more concrete, what are just some examples of good positioning statements or just the positioned companies?
turns.zh: 为了更具体，就给几个好定位陈述或定位好的公司的例子？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So one thing is a lot of times people will send me a link to their homepage and they'll say, "What do you think? Is this positioning good or not?" And the problem with B2B tech companies is, well, unless I'm your buyer, I'm not the right person to ask.
turns.zh: 一件事是，人们常发他们主页链接给我说「你觉得咋样？这定位好不？」而 B2B 科技公司的问题是，除非我是你的买家，我不是问这个的合适的人。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So you can have companies, people will say, "Well, I looked at the website and who knows what that is?" And it's like, well, it doesn't matter if I can understand what it is or not. If I'm selling a deeply technical thing to deeply technical buyers, it's okay if your grandmother doesn't understand what it is when they get there. What matters is, does it resonate for your buyers? And when they land there, do they go, "Oh yeah, I get what this is, and that seems like a thing I should have."
turns.zh: 所以你可能有公司，人们「嗯我看网站，谁知道那是啥？」而那是「嗯，我懂不懂那是啥不重要」。如果我卖很深的技术东西给很深的技术买家，你奶奶到了那不懂那是啥 OK。重要的是它 resonate 你的买家吗？他们落到那，会不会「哦对，我懂这是啥，而且那像是该有的东西」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so a lot of the companies that I really love the positioning of, you would go and look at it and say, "I don't know, man, I'm not even sure I really understand what that is." If you didn't have anything to do with APIs and you didn't know what the fuck an API was, whatever, you might land on Postman's page and go, "I honestly don't get that." But that's okay, you're not a person building the APIs, so you don't have to understand it. That's all right.
turns.zh: 所以我真爱的那些定位，你去看会说「我不知道啊哥们，我甚至不确定我真懂那是啥」。如果你跟 API 无关、你不知道 API 他妈是啥，whatever，你落到 Postman 页面会「老实说我真不懂」。但那 OK，你不是建 API 的人，所以你不必懂。都行。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Particularly, I've worked a lot with companies doing deep AI stuff, deep, deep digital analytics and deep data stuff and you can't tell from looking at the website, whether it's working or not. The true test of whether the positioning's working or not is, if I'm sitting across from a qualified prospect and I tell the story, does the prospect get excited and want to buy something? That's the real test of it.
turns.zh: 特别是，我跟很多做深度 AI、深度数字分析、深度数据的公司合作过，你看网站看不出它工作不工作。定位工作不工作的真正测试是：如果我坐在一个合格潜在客户对面、我讲这故事，潜在客户会兴奋、想买东西吗？那才是真正的测试。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Any other test I think is we're bringing our own baggage into it and saying ... I pick on these guys a little bit, but in Canada, there's a big startup conference, it's great, it's called Startupfest. It's in Montreal.
turns.zh: 任何其他测试我觉得都是我们带自己的 baggage 进去说……我老 pick on 这帮人，但在加拿大有个大创业会议，超棒，叫 Startupfest，在蒙特利尔。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've been to that.
turns.zh: 我去过。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: But every year they have this thing and it's called Pitch the Grannies. And you go in and you're a startup and you pitch the grandmothers and the grandmothers decide whether or not your pitch was any good. And this infuriates me because I'm like, "This is a terrible judge of pitching." Maybe if we're doing the VC pitch, in which case you're saying the VCs and the grandmothers are exactly the same, that's a little insulting.
turns.zh: 但每年他们有个东西叫 Pitch the Grannies（向奶奶们 pitch）。你进去，你是创业公司，你向奶奶们 pitch，奶奶们决定你的 pitch 好不好。这把我气疯，因为我想「这是对 pitch 的烂评判」。也许如果我们做 VC pitch，那 case 你说 VC 和奶奶完全一样，那有点 insulting。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: But certainly, if the pitch is a customer facing pitch, I don't care whether the grandmother understands it or not. Unless I happen to be building the thing for grandmas, I really don't think that matters at all, so yeah.
turns.zh: 但当然，如果 pitch 是面向客户的，我不在乎奶奶懂不懂。除非我碰巧是给奶奶建东西，我真觉得那一点都不重要，所以 yeah。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hopefully no B2B startups are pitching to grandmas, don't think that would go well.
turns.zh: 希望没有 B2B 创业公司在向奶奶 pitch，觉得那不会顺利。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so say that you're a PM or a founder that's ready to start figuring out their positioning for their product, what's the first thing that you do?
turns.zh: 好，假设你是 PM 或创始人，准备好开始搞清楚你产品的定位，你做的第一件事是什么？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So I've done a lot of thinking about how should we actually do positioning. And so a critical piece of positioning is your differentiated value, what's the value that you can deliver that no other company can deliver?
turns.zh: 所以我对「我们到底该怎么实操做定位」想了很多。定位的关键一块是你的差异化价值——你能交付、别的公司都交付不了的价值是啥？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so how companies get this wrong a lot is they'll say, "Okay, well, we want to look at our positioning, so let's get everybody together." Or sometimes they'll say, "Let's just sit in the marketing department and think about the value."
turns.zh: 公司常搞错的是，他们说「好，我们想看我们的定位，让所有人聚一起」。或有时他们说「让市场部坐那想想价值」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: But sometimes folks will get a team together, they get a team together and then they'll say, "Okay, so why does everybody love our stuff?" And this is a terrible way to go about it because what you'll get is just a bunch of opinions and we don't really know how to measure is that good or not.
turns.zh: 但有时人们把团队聚一起，然后说「好，为什么大家都爱我们的东西？」这是超糟的做法，因为你会得到一堆意见，而我们真不知道怎么衡量那好不好。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So I actually think the first step in a good positioning exercise is to really understand, what do we have to position against? So put another way, it's like saying, what do I have to beat in order to win a deal? So in positioning work we call this competitive alternatives.
turns.zh: 所以我其实觉得好的定位 exercise 的第一步是真正理解：我们要对什么做定位？换种说法，就像说，为了赢一个单子，我得打败啥？在定位工作里我们叫这个「竞争替代方案」(competitive alternatives)。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Now how people mess up this first step is I say competitive alternatives and they think competition, so things that look exactly like me. But in B2B, we have two sets of competitors. We have status quo, which is whatever the company is doing to attempt to solve the problem right now, even if it's crappy and not great.
turns.zh: 人们怎么搞砸这第一步：我说竞争替代方案，他们想成 competition，也就是长得 exact 像我的东西。但在 B2B，我们有两组竞争者。一组是现状——公司现在为试图解决问题做的任何事，即便它烂、不怎么样。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And then there's if the company does decide they're going to buy something different, they usually make a short list, so it's whoever else lands on the short list. So I need to be able to put a stake in the ground and say, "I got to beat all that in order to win a deal."
turns.zh: 另一组是，如果公司真决定买点不同的，他们通常做个短名单，所以谁进了短名单谁就算。所以我得能立个桩说「为了赢一个单子，我得打败所有这些」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Now, most folks will discount the status quo, but they shouldn't because in B2B we lose about 40% of our deals to quote-unquote, "no decision," which actually means we lost to the spreadsheet, we lost to pen and paper, we lost to interns. And if we're not positioning well against that, we're never going to get the customer to come off of that.
turns.zh: 现在大多数人会 discount 现状，但他们不该，因为在 B2B 我们大概 40% 的单子输给了「不做决定」——而那其实意思是我们输给了电子表格、输给了纸笔、输给了实习生。如果我们没对那个做好定位，我们永远没法让客户从那上面下来。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So I got to win against status quo, but I also have to win, if it's ... Most of the time, if it's B2B, you don't just buy the first thing you come across, you make a short list of alternatives and I got to win against those as well.
turns.zh: 所以我得赢过现状，但也得赢——如果……大多数时候，如果是 B2B，你不会只买你碰到的第一个东西，你会做个替代方案短名单，我也得赢过那些。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So step number one, what am I positioning against? Once I have that stake in the ground, then I can start thinking about what makes us different. So the easiest way to do this is okay, this is what I have to position against, what have I got capabilities wise that the alternatives don't have?
turns.zh: 所以第一步，我在对什么做定位？一旦我立了桩，我就能开始想什么让我们不同。最容易的方式是：好，这是我要对着的，我在能力上有什么替代方案没有的？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So feature, function, or even capabilities of the company, which could be pricing or professional services or other things that you've got, but also capabilities of the product. What have I got that the alternatives don't have? And I can make a giant list of these things.
turns.zh: 功能、或甚至公司的能力——可能是定价、专业服务、或其他你有的——但也是产品的能力。我有啥替代方案没有的？我能列张超长的单子。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And then I can translate that stuff into value by going down the list and saying, "Okay, we have this great feature, so what? Why does a customer care about it? What is the value that feature enables?" And when I do that mapping over to value, what generally happens is I end up with two or three value buckets or value themes.
turns.zh: 然后我把那些翻译成价值：走那张单子说「好，我们有这超棒功能，那又怎样？客户为什么在乎它？那功能带来的价值是啥？」当我做那个到价值的映射，通常发生的是我 end up 有两三个价值桶或价值主题。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And quite often those value buckets or value themes are different than what I would've gotten, if I got all the smart people in my company together and said, "Hey, why does everybody love our stuff?" When I do it this way, I'm ensured that those value themes are differentiated and not just things that are generally valuable, but any alternative could get it done, so why are we even talking about it? So in my mind, that's how we do it.
turns.zh: 而那些价值桶或价值主题，常不同于如果我把公司里所有聪明人聚一起说「嘿为什么大家都爱我们的东西」会得到的。用我这方式，我确保那些价值主题是差异化的，不只是「 generally 有价值但任何替代方案都能搞定」的东西——那我们聊它干嘛？所以在我心里，那是我们怎么做。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Once I've got differentiated value, then I can start thinking about, well, look, I could sell this product to any company that has this problem, but not everybody cares about this value the same way. And so what are the characteristics of a target account that make them really, really care a lot about that value? If I do some deep thinking about that, that's going to be my definition of a really best fit customer.
turns.zh: 一旦我有差异化价值，我能开始想：嗯，我能把这产品卖给任何有这问题的公司，但不是每个人都在乎这价值同等方式。所以，什么特征的目标客户会让他们非常、非常在乎那价值？如果我深想这个，那就是我对「最佳契合客户」的定义。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And then the last piece of positioning of course, is market category. And so again, a lot of people will just start with market category and then try to back up, which I think is crazy, because then we don't have any way to judge the goodness of a market category.
turns.zh: 然后定位最后一块当然是市场品类。所以 again，很多人直接从市场品类开始然后试图倒推，我觉得那疯了，因为那样我们没有任何方式判断一个市场品类好不好。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: But if I've got, look, this is the value only I can deliver, these are the kind of people that really care a lot about that value, if I start thinking about positioning as the context I position my product in, then the best market category is the context I position my product in such that this value is obvious to these people.
turns.zh: 但如果我有——看，这是只有我能交付的价值，这些是真正在乎那价值的那种人——如果我把定位想成我放产品的语境，那么最好的市场品类就是那个让我的价值对这些人 obvious 的语境。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: This is my long-winded way of doing it, but this is the only way I know how to get positioning done.
turns.zh: 这是我啰嗦的做法，但这是我唯一知道的把定位做完的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you just basically went through the steps and the bullet points of things you've got to figure out your position. Could you just briefly summarize that just for people to have that in their brain?
turns.zh: 你刚基本走了一遍步骤和你得搞清楚的要点。能简单总结一下，让人脑子里有？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Yeah. So it works like this. I start with competitive alternatives. What do I got to beat in order to win a deal, status quo, things on the short list. Once I've got that, then I can make a list of differentiated capabilities, what capabilities do I have that the alternatives do not? I can then translate those capabilities into value, the so what for the customer. And while I'm doing that, these things will theme out. So I'll end up with two, three value themes, value buckets.
turns.zh: 对。它这样工作。我从竞争替代方案开始。为了赢单子我得打败啥？现状、短名单上的。一旦我有那，我能列差异化能力——我有而替代方案没有的能力。然后我能把那些能力翻译成价值——对客户的「那又怎样」。我这么做时，这些事会 theme out，所以我 end up 有两三个价值主题、价值桶。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Once I have that, then I can ask myself the question, well, okay, what are the characteristics of a target account that make them care a lot about that value? So that next piece is best fit customers or target customers, who am I going after for this thing? And then the last bit's market category, so what's the context I position this thing in that makes my value obvious to the people I'm going after?
turns.zh: 一旦我有那个，我能问自己：好，什么特征的目标客户让他们非常在乎那价值？所以下一块是最佳契合客户或目标客户——我为这东西打谁？然后最后一块是市场品类——所以我把它放在啥语境里让我打的那帮人 obvious 地看到我的价值？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super helpful. What if we pick a company either that you worked with or that's just out there and think through what they would do for each of these steps to make this super real?
turns.zh: 超有帮助。如果我们挑个你合作过的、或就在市面上的公司，走一遍每一步他们会怎么做，让它超真实？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Sure. I'm going to do Help Scout because I like these guys.
turns.zh: 行。我要用 Help Scout，因为我喜欢这帮人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds good.
turns.zh: 听起来好。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And I was just talking to the CEO not too long ago. So Help Scout's a good example in that they're a startup. I would call them a growth stage startup. They're not super big, but they're not teeny-weeny either. And they're in what would appear to be a terrible market, which is they sell software for customer success. So their competitor's like Zendesk. There's actually a million companies in this space, but the gorilla in the market is Zendesk.
turns.zh: 我不久前刚跟他们 CEO 聊过。Help Scout 是个好例子，他们是个创业公司。我会叫他们增长期创业公司。他们不算超大，但也不 tiny。他们在看着很糟的市场——他们卖客服软件。所以他们的竞争者像 Zendesk。这领域其实有一百万家公司，但市场里的 gorilla 是 Zendesk。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so if I put the stake in the ground and say, "Well, what do I got to replace?" Well, their customer's a lot of small, medium businesses, a lot of direct to consumer E-commerce businesses. And so they obviously have to beat Zendesk and the other folks that are out there, but sometimes they're replacing just email or even a rudimentary shared inbox. That's who they got to beat.
turns.zh: 所以如果我把桩立下说「好，我得替换啥？」他们的客户很多是中小企、很多是 DTC 电商。所以他们显然得打败 Zendesk 和其他人，但有时他们在替换的只是 email、甚至 rudimentary 共享收件箱。那是他们得打败的。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so when you look through what Help Scout has that's differentiating, they've got a whole bunch of features that are really around delivering really amazing service to the customer. So they do a shared inbox. They were the first ones to do a proper services-oriented shared inbox to make sure that nobody gets missed and the right people get assigned to the right thing and you don't get conflicts.
turns.zh: 当你看 Help Scout 有的差异化，他们有一堆功能，都是关于给客户交付真的惊艳的服务。他们做共享收件箱。他们是第一个做 proper 面向服务的共享收件箱——确保没人被漏掉、对的人分到对的事、没有冲突。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: But they do a lot of other things like their whole philosophy about how they treat a customer in the service process is really different from Zendesk. So you get assigned a ticket number, you get assigned a person and things like that. And so they do all the neat, integrated things like they'll do a chat bot thing, but it only appears when there's an actual person to chat with you. They don't try to pretend they're a machine, things like that. So they want to guarantee a really high level of service.
turns.zh: 但他们做很多别的——比如他们对待服务过程中客户的整个哲学跟 Zendesk 很不同。你拿到的是 ticket 号、分到个人之类的。他们做所有 neat 的集成东西，比如做聊天机器人，但只在真有活人能跟你聊时才出现。他们不假装自己是机器，之类。所以他们想保证超高的服务水平。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So when you map that to value, the value is one, I'm delivering this extra amazing service for customers. I'm not trying to push customers to a low cost channel. I'm treating them like a person. So their value is really around delivering amazing customer service that's going to deepen your relationship with the customer. That's the value.
turns.zh: 所以当你把那映射到价值，价值一是：我给客户交付这额外的惊艳服务。我不是把客户推向低成本渠道。我把他们当人对待。所以他们的价值真围绕「交付惊艳客服，深化你跟客户的关系」。那是价值。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And then you say, "Well, who cares a lot about that?" Well, not everybody. So there are businesses out there, I would argue maybe your phone company doesn't really care. They have a giant call center and all they care about is reducing the cost in their call center and driving you to low cost channels.
turns.zh: 然后你说「好，谁非常在乎那个？」嗯，不是所有人。有些企业——我 argue 你的电话公司可能真不在乎。他们有 giant 呼叫中心，只在乎压低呼叫中心成本、把你推向低成本渠道。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: They don't actually see customer service as a way to build a relationship with you versus a lot of direct to consumer brands or E-commerce brands. This is almost the only way that they can interact with their customer. So they actually see customer service as a way to really drive growth through customer loyalty. And so those are the kind of companies that are a really good fit for Help Scout.
turns.zh: 他们不真把客服看成建关系的方式，而很多 DTC 或电商品牌，这几乎是他们跟客户互动的唯一方式。所以他们真把客服看成通过客户忠诚驱动增长的方式。所以那类是 Help Scout 很契合的公司。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So I go through that process, that's my positioning. Then the next thing you got to do is okay, now that I understand all that, how do I weave a story around that? So how do I tell the story about that, if a customer comes to me? And so what we want to do with our positioning is turn it into a sales narrative that clicks with the kind of customers we know we can sell to.
turns.zh: 所以我走那个流程，那是我的定位。然后你要做的下件事是：好，既然我懂了所有那个，我怎么织个故事 around 那个？如果客户来找我，我怎么讲那个故事？所以我们想用定位做的是，把它变成跟我们能卖的那种客户 click 的销售叙事。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So the way Help Scout delivers the story, if you come in, you're a qualified prospect, it starts with this idea that customer success is a growth driver. Modern E-commerce companies see customer success as a way to deepen customer relationships, increase repeat buying, show it as a growth driver. And they have a bunch of great stats that prove that this is true.
turns.zh: Help Scout 交付故事的方式：如果你进来，你是合格潜在客户，它从「客户成功是增长引擎」这个点子开始。现代电商公司把客户成功看成深化客户关系、增加复购、显示它是增长引擎的方式。他们有一堆很棒的 stats 证明那是真的。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And then they go look at all your other alternatives. All your other alternatives treat your people like a number. They give them a number. They try to drive them to low cost channels. They try to do these things. They are not treating this like a growth driver, they're treating it like a cost center.
turns.zh: 然后他们去看你所有其他替代方案。你所有其他替代方案把你的人当数字。他们给你个数字。他们试图把你推向低成本渠道。他们试图做这些事。他们不把这当增长引擎，他们当成本中心。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so being able to tell that story that takes your differentiated value and puts it into context is the way all this stuff comes together and the rubber meets the road. So I don't know if that's a good example.
turns.zh: 所以能讲那个把你的差异化价值放进语境的故事，是这一切合到一起、橡胶接地的方式。我不知道那是不是好例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, that's an amazing example. That makes it so real. Is the output of this process a doc with these bullet points, plus this story that you train sales on? Or how does that look?
turns.zh: 哦，那例子超棒。让它超真实。这流程的产物是一份有这些要点的 doc、加上你训练销售用的故事吗？还是长啥样？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Yeah. So we do two things in the workshops that I do. So first we get the gang together. So I want representation from sales, marketing, product, customer success, CEO, everybody in the room together. And then we're going to work through the five piece parts.
turns.zh: 对。所以在我做的工作坊里我们做两件事。第一，我们把帮派聚一起。我要销售、市场、产品、客户成功、CEO、所有人都在屋里。然后我们走那五块。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So once we've got, here's what we compete with, here's how we're different, this is the value we can deliver no one else can, these are the kind of people that really love our stuff, so here's who we're going after, this is the market we're going to win, then we can document that in a document.
turns.zh: 一旦我们有了——这是我们竞争的、这是我们不同的、这是我们能交付别人不能的价值、这些是真爱我们东西的那种人所以这是我们打谁、这是我们要赢的市场——然后我们能把那记进一份文档。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And for the marketing people, that's a good starting place to then go and build messaging because we've got an idea what our value props are. But if we end there and we just stop there, then what usually happens is the rest of the team goes back to normal and they go, "Yeah, we did this thing." And conceptually they get it, but they don't know how to tell a story. It's super important in sales because if sales can't tell the story, they can't pitch it, if they can't pitch it, they're going to make shit up.
turns.zh: 对市场人，那是去建 messaging 的好起点，因为我们有了价值主张的 idea。但如果我们停在那、就停那，通常发生的是团队其他人回到正常，说「嗯我们做了这事」。概念上他们懂，但他们不知道怎么讲故事。这在销售里超重要，因为如果销售不会讲故事，他们就不能 pitch，不能 pitch 他们就会瞎编。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so what we want to do then is, okay, we've got this positioning, now let's put it together into a sales narrative that we can then take and test with qualified prospects and make sure it works, but we've also got something that the sales team can pitch and oh, by the way, everybody else knows how to tell the story too. So product knows how to tell the story, customer success knows how to tell the story, CEO knows how to tell the story.
turns.zh: 所以我们想做的是：好，我们有这定位了，现在让我们把它拼成一份销售叙事，我们能拿去跟合格潜在客户测、确保它工作，但我们也有了销售团队能 pitch 的东西——哦顺带，其他所有人都知道怎么讲故事了。所以产品知道怎么讲、客户成功知道怎么讲、CEO 知道怎么讲。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So the last thing we do is we map this positioning to a sales narrative. So what we do in the workshop is we storyboard it out. And then after the workshop is done, the team's going, usually it's marketing and sales together, they take that storyboard and then turn it into an actual pitch, which is like a deck, a demo, a script. And then they can use that to test the positioning as well.
turns.zh: 所以我们最后做的事是，我们把这定位映射到销售叙事。工作坊里我们把它 storyboard 出来。工作坊结束后，团队——通常是市场和销售一起——拿那个 storyboard 变成实际的 pitch，像 deck、demo、script。然后他们也能用它测定位。
