turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So the output ends up being an actual pitch or a story they tell on sales calls, forms the way they marketing position or talks about the company. There's two questions I want to ask. I want to make sure I don't forget.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以产物最后是个实际的 pitch、或他们在销售电话上讲的故事，形成他们市场定位或聊公司的方式。有两个问题我想问。我想确保别忘了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One is about messaging versus positioning. But maybe before that, it's interesting that positioning starts with focusing on your differentiator. Is that essential for a company to always figure out a differentiator and be different? Or are there examples where maybe you don't need to focus on that?
turns.zh: 一个是 messaging vs 定位。但也许在那之前，有意思的是定位从聚焦你的不同点开始。公司总是得搞清楚一个不同点、变得不同，是必须的吗？还是有没有例子你不必聚焦那个？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Well, what you want to do is you want to take a customer's viewpoint on this, right? So let's think about how customers buy. We don't talk about this a lot, but let's think about how customers buy. Typical B2B buying process, this is what it looks like.
turns.zh: 嗯，你想做的是从客户的观点看这事，对吧？所以想想客户怎么买。我们不太聊这个，但想想客户怎么买。典型 B2B 购买流程，长这样。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Somebody, VP sales wakes up in the morning and says, "You know what sucks? The way we track our pipeline sucks. It's stupid. I can't deal with this anymore. We need to get a tool in here. We should have a CRM, man." And they go to the office and they don't actually go look for the new tool. They find some sucker in the office like John, you, get out there, manager of sales ops or whatever, find us a CRM.
turns.zh: 某人，销售 VP 早上起来说「你知道啥烂？我们跟 pipeline 的方式烂。蠢。我受不了了。我们得在这搞个工具。我们该有个 CRM，哥们」。然后他去办公室，他其实没去找新工具。他找办公室里某个 suckers 像 John——你，出去，销售运营经理或 whatever，给我们找个 CRM。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And John's panicked. John's like, "Oh my God, you're kidding me." Maybe John's used some CRMs, but he's not an expert on the CRM market. He doesn't know what's possible and what isn't possible. So John's like, "Oh God, I don't even know." And then he Googles and what does he get? A fire hose of information.
turns.zh: John 慌了。John 想「哦我的天，你开玩笑吧」。也许 John 用过一些 CRM，但他不是 CRM 市场专家。他不知道什么可能、什么不可能。所以 John 想「哦天我甚至不知道」。然后他谷歌，得到啥？消防水管一样的信息。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: He goes on a G2 Crowd and Software Advice and all these places. There's 9,000 companies listed, they're all in the top ranked quadrant. There's like a thousand of them. Some of them are for big companies. Some of them are small companies. I have no idea how to make a short list, freaking out.
turns.zh: 他去 G2 Crowd、Software Advice 和所有地方。列了 9000 家公司，都在 top ranked 象限。大概有上千家。有些给大公司，有些给小公司。我完全不知道怎么做短名单，freaking out。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so somehow they figure out how to make a short list and that person has got to justify this choice to their boss, so there better be something there. I'm not allowed to just throw the dart at it. I'm not allowed to just go back to my VP and say, "I just like the rep better, man. They're all the same. I picked this one by spinning the wheel." No, you got to go back and tell your boss why you made a smart choice.
turns.zh: 所以 somehow 他们搞出怎么做短名单，而那人得向老板 justify 这选择，所以那得有点东西在那。我不能就扔飞镖。我不能就回去跟 VP 说「我就更喜欢那销售代表，哥们。他们都一样。我转轮盘选的」。不，你得回去跟你老板说你为啥做了个聪明选择。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so we have to be able to give customers that when they get on the sales call with us. The best thing we could do is say, "Look, buddy, there's lots of CRMs out there, and let me tell you how this market shakes out. These ones are really good for big enterprises. These ones are really good, if you got this. These ones are really good, if you got this. But look, if you're this, this and this, you really need these four things and we got that and that's why you should pick us."
turns.zh: 所以我们得能在客户跟我们销售电话时给他们那个。我们最该做的是说「看，哥们，外面一堆 CRM，让我告诉你这市场怎么分。这些对大企业真 good。这些对如果你有这个真 good。这些对如果你有这个真 good。但看，如果你是这样、这样、这样，你真需要这四样东西，而我们有，那就是你该选我们的原因」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Because we need to make that customer feel comfortable they've made a good decision. Otherwise, what happens? No decision, that's what happens. If they can't figure that out, they go back to the boss and say, "You know what? All the CRMs are shit. We should just keep using the spreadsheet. It's fine. Let's just allay this." And 40% of the time that's what happened.
turns.zh: 因为我们需要让那客户舒服地觉得做了个好决定。否则发生啥？不做决定，就那样。如果他们搞不懂，他们回去跟老板说「你知道啥？所有 CRM 都屎。我们该继续用电子表格。挺好。我们就 allay 这」。而 40% 的时候那就是发生的。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So if you can't help the customer figure out how to justify this decision and make this decision and basically come back and say, "I decided this was the right approach to the problem and I picked this one for this reason," then you're not going to get the deal and nobody's going to get the deal.
turns.zh: 所以如果你不能帮客户搞清楚怎么 justify 这决定、做这决定、基本回去说「我决定这是对问题的正确方法、我因这原因选了这个」，那你就拿不到单子，谁都拿不到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And in your experience, the fact that here's why it's different from maybe the incumbents or other options ends up being really important? Basically, it's really hard to win by just saying we're better, say better than Slack or better than Zoom. It needs to be-
turns.zh: 在你的经验里，这里有个「为什么它跟 incumbent 或其他选项不同」最后变得超重要？基本上，只说「我们更好」——比如比 Slack 或比 Zoom 好——很难赢。它需要是——

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: But better how? You got to be able to articulate better. So sometimes it's like they have more bells and whistles, but we're simpler and you don't actually need all those bells and whistles. So we're better because we're easier at it, less training, easier to get stood up, whatever.
turns.zh: 但好在哪？你得能 articlate 好。有时像他们有更多花里胡哨，但我们更简单、你其实不需要那些花里胡哨。所以我们更好因为我们更容易、培训更少、更容易立起来，whatever。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Or you might say the opposite of that, we have all the bells and whistles. It's super customizable. You could do whatever you want. Those other things are Mickey Mouse play things. You're a big mature company, you need all the bells and whistles. We're better.
turns.zh: 或者你可能说相反的：我们有所有花里胡哨。超可定制。你想干啥都行。那些其他东西是 Mickey Mouse 玩具。你是成熟大公司，你需要所有花里胡哨。我们更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: Great。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so that better has two pieces to it, what's the value and who cares about that value? Because better means something different to different segments in the market. So better for a small company is not the same thing as better for a large enterprise.
turns.zh: 所以那个「更好」有两块：价值是啥、谁在乎那个价值？因为「更好」对市场不同细分意味着不同的事。所以对小公司的「更好」不等于对大企业的「更好」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Your trick in the positioning is to be able to articulate, why are we the best kind of solution for this particular type of customer? That's it. And if you could nail that, then you sell lots of stuff, you beat the other guys, you win deals all the time.
turns.zh: 你定位里的诀窍是能 articlate：为什么我们是对这类客户最好的解决方案？就这。如果你能钉死那个，你就卖一堆东西、你打败别人、你一直赢单。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. That's going to be our soundbite from this episode maybe.
turns.zh: 我爱那个。那可能是这集的 soundbite。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Oh great.
turns.zh: 哦好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There it is. I want to go back to the messaging versus positioning. What's the difference between those two concepts?
turns.zh: 在那呢。我想回到 messaging vs 定位。这两个概念区别是啥？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So they get confused a lot and a lot of people will say, "Well, I don't like our messaging. So can you come in and help do messaging?" I think they're really distinct because I see positioning as a fundamental input to messaging.
turns.zh: 它们常被混，很多人会说「嗯我不喜欢我们的 messaging。所以你能来帮做 messaging 吗？」我觉得它们真不同，因为我把定位看成 messaging 的基础输入。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Most of the time when people say messaging, what they mean is this is the text on the homepage, which is really different from what is my definition of competitive alternative? How do we win in the market? Where do we win in the market? So positioning's all about defining that and then things flow out of that. So I can't write the messaging until I understand, well, who's the message for, and what's our value against who? And so once I understand all of that, then I can understand how to write messaging.
turns.zh: 大多数时候人们说 messaging，意思是主页上的文字，那真不同于「我的竞争替代方案是啥？我们怎么在市场赢？我们在市场哪赢？」所以定位全是定义那个，然后东西从那流出来。所以我不能在理解「嗯，这 message 给谁、我们对谁的价值是啥」之前写 messaging。一旦我懂了所有那个，我才能懂怎么写 messaging。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: A lot of people get confused between positioning and branding as well. And folks will sometimes use those words interchangeably or they'll talk about brand positioning, which really bugs me. I mean, there's positioning and there's branding, those two things are different.
turns.zh: 很多人也把定位和品牌搞混。人们有时互换用那些词、或聊「品牌定位」，那真烦我。我的意思是，有定位、有品牌，那两件事不同。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: But if I was going to work on branding, again, I can't figure out what I want the brand to stand for until I understand, well, who's my target buyer and what's my differentiation from the other alternatives in the market because I want that brand to be distinct.
turns.zh: 但如果我要做品牌，again，在我理解「嗯我的目标买家是谁、我跟市场上其他替代方案的差异化是啥」之前，我没法搞清我想让品牌代表啥，因为我要那品牌 distinct。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So I need to have positioning figured out first and then practically everything I do in marketing and sales flows downstream from that.
turns.zh: 所以我得先把定位搞清楚，然后 practically 我在市场和销售做的一切都从那下游流出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there any companies out there that you think need help with their positioning that maybe have an opportunity to work with someone like you?
turns.zh: 有没有你觉得需要定位帮助、可能有机会跟像你这样的人合作的公司？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: There's some companies that I think you can tell they've not really thought about it. And a lot of times you'll see it in companies where they're brand new and the tech is really spectacular, but you can tell they haven't quite figured out well, so what?
turns.zh: 有些公司你能看出他们没真想过。很多时候你在很新、技术超炫的公司看到，但你能看出他们没真搞清楚「那又怎样？」

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So when Magic Leap first launched that stuff was so mind blowing and it was like, oh my gosh, and all their demonstrations, the thing with the elephant and the guy's hand and all that stuff, and you're like, "Wow, that's amazing."
turns.zh: 所以 Magic Leap 刚发布时那东西超 mind blowing，什么大象、那人的手之类的演示，你「哇超棒」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And I read this really in depth interview with the founder and he was talking about the tech and this guy's view on the market, it was so interesting, but it was like, so what? What am I actually going to do with that? Who's your target market for this? What is the value of this? We all get it's cool, but what is the actual value of this?
turns.zh: 我读了个超深入的创始人访谈，他聊技术、这人对市场的看法，超有趣，但就像，那又怎样？我实际要拿它干啥？你的目标市场是谁？这的价值是啥？我们都懂它酷，但它的实际价值是啥？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And you can see now, which I don't know if people know this, but if you go to the Magic Leap site, and I do because I'm interested in Magic Leap because I've been following their story since the beginning, but they've now gotten much tighter on their positioning.
turns.zh: 你现在能看到——我不知道人们知不知道——但如果你去 Magic Leap 网站，因为我对它感兴趣，我从一开始跟它的故事，他们现在定位紧多了。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And they're actually selling B2B now, into manufacturing and they're talking about wide frame of view and all this stuff you can do, that's really differentiated than you could with other types of traditional VR things. And so if you look at their positioning, now, it's getting much, much tighter, but at the beginning it was like, what?
turns.zh: 他们现在真在卖 B2B，进制造业，聊宽视场角和你用传统 VR 做不了的各种事——那真差异化。所以你看他们定位，现在紧多了，但一开始是「啥？」

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And I felt the same thing about Google Glass, when it first came out. It was like, I get why people get excited about it, I just don't get why anybody would buy. I get what it is, but why do we need one of those? I don't see the value in this thing at all.
turns.zh: Google Glass 刚出时我也有同感。我懂人们为啥兴奋，我就是不懂为啥有人会买。我懂它是啥，但为啥我们需要一个？我完全看不到这东西的价值。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And then again, if you see the applications for Google Glass now, there's a lot of very specific B2B use cases that they're now doubling down on. And they're coming back to the consumer use case a little bit now for some augmented reality stuff that actually sounds like it's useful. But a lot of times what we'll get is the initial launch of something will be this gee-whiz, it's so amazing.
turns.zh: 然后 again，你看 Google Glass 现在的应用，有很多非常具体的 B2B 用例他们在加倍下注。他们现在稍微回到消费者用例，做些听起来真有用的 AR 东西。但很多时候，一个东西的初始发布会是这种 gee-whiz、超惊人。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: The archetype of this is the launch of the Segway. So there's been a couple of books written about it, but it's fascinating. The original founder of the Segway was the Elon Musk of his day. He had done three or four other companies, they were all wildly successful. When he got the idea for the Segway, he literally lifted his little pinky and raised a hundred million from Steve Jobs, Jeff Bezos, and a who's who of Silicon Valley venture.
turns.zh: 这个的 archetype 是 Segway 的发布。有几本书写过它，但迷人。Segway 原创始人是我们那天的 Elon Musk。他做过三四个其他公司，都超成功。当他有 Segway 的点子，他 literally 翘小指从 Steve Jobs、Jeff Bezos 和硅谷名人录融了一亿。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And then he kept positioning the thing as a revolution in human transport, but he didn't want to let the cat out of the bag, what it was, so he just kept saying that. And he was in the news all over and he's like, "Revolution in human transport." And people were getting so excited because they were like, "What's a revolution in human transport? It's a flying car, man. We're finally getting flying cars."
turns.zh: 然后他一直把那东西定位成「人类交通的革命」，但他不想让猫出袋、说它是啥，所以他一直那么说。他上了所有新闻，说「人类交通的革命」。人们超兴奋，因为「人类交通的革命是啥？是飞行汽车，哥们。我们终于有飞行汽车了」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So everybody's studying his patent filings and all this stuff, and they were like, "Oh my God, we're getting flying cars. It's going to be amazing." And there was such hype around this thing when they launched it that he actually got invited to Good Morning America.
turns.zh: 所以每个人都研究他的专利文件之类的，想「哦我的天我们要有飞行汽车了。会超棒」。发布时 hype 大到他真被邀上 Good Morning America。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was watching that. I was watching that live [inaudible 00:41:33]-
turns.zh: 我当时在看。我 live 看的——

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Yeah, to come on Good Morning America, do the thing and everyone's like, "Oh my God, we're getting flying cars." And then he comes out on the Segway and everyone's like, "What the fuck? That's not what we were promised, man."
turns.zh: 对，上 Good Morning America 做那个，每个人都「哦我的天我们要有飞行汽车了」。然后他踩着 Segway 出来，每个人都「搞啥？那不是承诺我们的东西，哥们」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And the interesting thing about this Segway was that refusal to position it at a micro level, left it up to the customers to decide what it was. So even when we saw it was like, "Okay, so it's human transport. We get that, but what should I compare it to? Should I compare it to a car or a bicycle?"
turns.zh: Segway 有意思的是，拒绝在微观层面定位它，把它留给客户决定它是啥。所以即便我们看到「好，它是人类交通。我们懂，但我该拿它跟啥比？跟车还是自行车比？」

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so a lot of the early users were saying it was the worst thing to have a Segway because nobody knew where you were supposed to drive it because they didn't know what it was. So if you were driving on the road, cars were honking at you and they're like, "Get that stupid thing off the road." But if you drive it on the sidewalk, then the ladies with the baby strollers are like, "Get that stupid thing off the sidewalk."
turns.zh: 所以很多早期用户说有 Segway 是最糟的事，因为没人知道你该在哪开它——他们不知道它是啥。所以如果你在路上开，车对你按喇叭「把那蠢东西开下路」。但如果你在人行道上开，推婴儿车的女士「把那蠢东西开下人行道」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And the thing was a colossal failure eventually. The patents are still amazing. The patents just got sold last year or the year before to some company that does these hoverboard things. But the tech was way, way ahead of its time, but there wasn't good positioning to answer the question, who's this for? Why do they care? So what?
turns.zh: 那东西最后是 colossal 失败。专利还是超棒。专利去年或前年卖给做 hoverboard 的公司了。但技术远超时代，却没有好定位回答「这是给谁的？他们为啥在乎？那又怎样？」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really good segue to a question I wanted to ask you is when-
turns.zh: 那是接去我想问你的问题的好 segue——当——

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Segue, ooh.
turns.zh: Segue，哦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Unintentionally intended. When does it make sense for a company to bring in someone like you to go deep on positioning?
turns.zh: 哇。unintentionally intended。公司啥时候该引入像你这样的人深做定位？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: I think most companies can do positioning on their own. That's my belief. Some companies I think lack a methodology to follow to go do it. So I wrote a book called Obviously Awesome, and that was the purpose of that book. If you want to do positioning and you just want to start a little exercise and do it yourself in house, you can use my methodology and my way to do it. And I think most companies can get it done that way.
turns.zh: 我觉得大多数公司能自己做完定位。那是我的信念。有些公司我觉得缺个能 follow 的方法论去做。所以我写了本《Obviously Awesome》，那本书的目的就是这个。如果你想做定位、只想开始个小 exercise 自己内部做，你可以用我的方法论和我做的方式。我觉得大多数公司那样能搞定。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: But most of the ones that come to me have attempted to do that and it hasn't worked out for one reason or another. So sometimes it's because, and this is not unusual in startups, we got an executive team full of A type people and we're all pretty opinionated and we just can't get to agreement on stuff. And it makes a lot of sense to bring an outside person in to help facilitate that conversation, particularly one that's got a lot of experience in positioning.
turns.zh: 但来找我的大多数试过那样、因为这样那样原因没成。有时因为——创业公司里不罕见——我们有个全是 A 型的高管团队，我们都挺有主见，就是没法对事达成一致。引入个外人帮 facilitate 那对话很有意义，尤其有定位经验的人。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So sometimes I get brought in for that reason. Other times I get brought in as companies just feel like they really got to nail it because there's a lot at stake. I've done a lot of work with companies that they're about to hire 10, 15 people in sales or they're about to make a really big investment in marketing and they just want to make sure they really nail it and not have to maybe do a not so great version and then redo it and then redo it again. If you bring me in, then we're going to nail it. There's no way we're going to get to something that isn't good.
turns.zh: 所以有时我因那原因被引入。其他时候公司引入我是因为他们觉得真得钉死它，因为 stakes 大。我跟很多快招 10、15 个销售、或快在营销上投大钱的公司做过，他们就想确保真钉死、不必做个不太好的版本然后重做、再重做。如果你引入我，那我们会钉死。我们绝不会弄出个不好的。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So sometimes people bring me in because they feel like there's a lot at stake. And those are generally the companies that bring me in. Some bigger companies I think bring me in, again, a bit more of a security blanket. We know we could do it ourselves, we kind of got it ourselves, but we'd feel better if we had the expert in here just to make sure we nail it once and we don't have to come back and do this again right away.
turns.zh: 所以有时人们因 stakes 大引入我。那一般是引入我的公司。有些大公司引入我，again，更像安全毯。我们知道自己能做、自己大概搞定了，但有个专家在这让我们安心一次钉死、不必马上回来重做。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So those are the kind of companies typically I work with, but I think a lot of companies could get it done with my book or some methodology, get the gang together and just bang it out themselves. I think everybody should start there.
turns.zh: 所以那通常是我合作的公司类型，但我觉得很多公司能用我的书或某方法论、把帮派聚一起自己 bang 出来。我觉得人人都该从那开始。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome. How long should it take to do this kind of process either on their own and then with you? How long do these things take?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这流程自己做完、或跟你做，各要多久？这些事花多久？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Well, so the work that I do, we do it as a week long sprint. Now there's a bunch of prep that happens before that and there's some stuff we do afterwards, but the actual exercise itself is a series of sessions spread out over a week. I've seen companies do it on their own and they do it in a couple of days. They trap everybody in a room over a couple of days.
turns.zh: 嗯，我做的工作，我们做成一个一周的 sprint。那之前有一堆 prep、之后有一些事，但 exercise 本身是 spread 在一周的系列 sessions。我看过公司自己做的，他们几天做完。他们把所有人关屋里几天。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Assuming you've got the right information to go and start with it, it shouldn't take you too long. And it really depends on how contentious things are because again, what you're trying to get to is agreement and alignment across the team. You're not done until everybody thinks what we've come up with is good.
turns.zh: 假设你有对的信息开始，不该花太久。真取决于东西多 contentious，因为 again，你想达到的是团队的一致和对齐。在所有人觉得我们搞出的东西好之前，你没完。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it sounds like you work mostly with larger companies and later stage companies. I mentioned this to you before we-
turns.zh: 听起来你主要跟更大的、更后期的公司合作。我之前跟你提过——

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Yes and no.
turns.zh: 是也不是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Okay.
turns.zh: 好。好。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Yes and no. It depends on how you define that really. I've done a lot of companies that are around 5 million revenue, 10 million revenue in there. So they're beyond seed stage, but I wouldn't call them a large company quite yet.
turns.zh: 是也不是。真看你咋定义。我做过很多大概 500 万、1000 万营收的公司。所以他们过了种子期，但我还不会叫他们大公司。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: But I will say this, I do get a lot of calls from companies that are super early stage and where I don't think they're ready to actually really ... Well, they're not ready to bring in someone like me, and I think in general, they're not ready to really over tighten their positioning.
turns.zh: 但我会说这个：我确实接到很多超早期公司的电话，而我觉得他们其实没准备好真……嗯，他们没准备好引入像我的人，而且我觉得 generally 他们没准备好真把定位收太紧。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So I think about it this way. So I've got this new thing, I'm either about to launch it into market or I've got it in market, I've got a handful of customers. At that stage, what I think you've got is a positioning thesis. And so the best thing you could do is deliberately go through a positioning exercise, document the thesis.
turns.zh: 所以我是这么想的。我有个新东西，我要么准备 launch 进市场、要么已经在市场里、有几个客户。在那个阶段，我觉得你有的叫「定位假设」(positioning thesis)。所以你能做的最好的事是刻意走一遍定位 exercise、把假设记下来。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so the thesis says, we think we compete with these folks. We think this is differentiating. This is the value we think we can deliver that no one else can. These are the people we think are going to get really excited about that. Therefore, this is the market we're going to win. But it's just a thesis.
turns.zh: 所以假设说：我们认为我们跟这帮人竞争。我们认为这是差异化的。这是我们认为能交付、别人不能的价值。这些是我们认为会超兴奋的人。因此，这是我们要赢的市场。但它只是个假设。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so internally it's good for us all to be in alignment internally, but when I go to launch that externally, if I don't have any customers yet, it's very likely, and in my experience, 100% of the time, the thesis is partially incorrect. It's based on a bunch of assumptions and our best guess at it, based on what we did in customer discovery or all our research we did before we built the thing.
turns.zh: 所以在内部，我们全对齐有好处，但当我要外部 launch 那个，如果我还没有任何客户，很可能——而且依我经验 100% 的时候——那假设部分错。它基于一堆假设、我们基于客户探索或建东西前做的研究的最佳猜测。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: But we always, we're never a hundred percent correct. And so in these cases, I actually think it's better in the early days of a product to keep the positioning a little bit loose and allow the market to pull you maybe in a direction that you didn't think it was going to.
turns.zh: 但我们从不 100% 对。所以在这些 case，我其实觉得产品早期保持定位稍微松一点更好，让市场把你拉向也许你没想到要去的 direction。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So here's my terrible analogy I use all the time, but I'm going to use it here. But it's like I designed a fishing net and my thesis is this thing's amazing for tuna. It's a tuna fishing net. It's the world's greatest tuna fishing net.
turns.zh: 所以这是我的烂类比，我总用，但我在这要用。它像我设计了个渔网，我的假设是这东西对金枪鱼超棒。它是金枪鱼渔网。世界最棒的金枪鱼渔网。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So I could launch that and say, "It's just for tuna, only tuna. Don't use it if it's not tuna." And maybe it works for tuna, maybe it doesn't and I don't really know. And if it fails, it fails hard.
turns.zh: 我能 launch 那个说「只给金枪鱼，只有金枪鱼。不是金枪鱼就别用」。也许它对金枪鱼工作，也许不，我真不知道。如果它失败，它 hard 失败。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: A better way I think is we know internally that it's the tuna fishing net. That's why we built it. That's what it is, but let's just at the beginning, let's put it out there and keep it a little loose and we say, "It's a net for fish, big fish, all kinds of big fish, any kind of big fish. And then let's just see, let's let the fishermen try it out. Let's see what they pull up."
turns.zh: 我觉得更好的方式是：我们知道内部它是金枪鱼渔网。那是我们建它的原因。那是它。但让我们开头就把它放出去、保持松一点，我们说「它是渔网，给鱼、大鱼、所有大鱼、任何大鱼。然后我们看，让渔民试试。看他们捞起啥」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And maybe what we discover is, you know what? This thing's actually amazing for grouper and we just didn't know, because we're not grouper people. We didn't really think about grouper. And then once we've got enough of that signal and we start seeing the pattern in who loves our stuff and why, then we can really tighten it up and run at that market.
turns.zh: 也许我们发现的是，你知道啥？这东西对石斑鱼 (grouper) 超棒，而我们就是不知道，因为我们不是石斑鱼人。我们没真想过石斑鱼。然后一旦我们有足够信号、开始看到谁爱我们东西、为啥的模式，我们就能真收紧它、冲那个市场。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: But at the beginning, I think it's actually okay if your positioning's a little bit loose. And so I think you can worry too much about positioning in the super early days of a product when it's impossible to tighten it up, because you just don't have the data to do it.
turns.zh: 但开头，我觉得你的定位松一点其实 OK。所以我觉你在产品超早期太担心定位是过度——那时不可能收紧，因为你就是没数据做它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that you touched on this a bit, but what does that transition look like between, okay, it's okay to keep it loose and see where the market pulls to, okay, we got to start taking this seriously? Is there a trigger that's like, okay, let's get into this?
turns.zh: 我知道你稍微聊过这个，但那个过渡长啥样——好，保持松、看市场拉向哪，好，我们得认真了？有没有个 trigger 像「好，我们进这个」？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Yeah. It's one of those things that usually like you know when you know. But what you want is you want to start feeling comfortable that there's a pattern and it isn't just like, hey, I got one customer in this segment and one customer in this segment and one customer in this segment and I don't really know.
turns.zh: 对。是那种你懂的时候就懂的事。但你想的是开始感觉舒服有个模式，而不是「嘿我在这细分有个客户、那细分有个客户、那细分有个客户，我真不知道」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: What it usually starts at the beginning is it starts with, you'll say, "Gosh, all kinds of people like our stuff. All kinds of people like our stuff for all kinds of different reasons." And if you're seeing that you don't see the pattern yet.
turns.zh: 它开头通常是：你说「天，各种人爱我们的东西。各种人因各种不同原因爱我们的东西」。如果你看到那，你还没看到模式。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And eventually what happens is the pattern starts becoming clear that it's like, oh, all those customers look differently but there's actually this thread through them. Look, they all have the same marketing automation tool. Isn't that interesting? Or they all have the same number of sales people on their team. Isn't that interesting? I've done enough of these pitches now to know if you've got this, this, and this, this pitch is going to go good, and if you don't, it is not going to go good.
turns.zh: 最终发生的是模式开始清晰——哦，那些客户看起来不同，但有个线穿过他们。看，他们都有同一个营销自动化工具。有意思？或他们团队都有同样数量的销售。有意思？我做过足够多这种 pitch 现在知道，如果你有这、这、这，这 pitch 会好；如果没有，它不会好。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So once you start feeling like I got the pattern here, it's starting to come into focus, then I think you're ready to really tighten things up, smash your foot on the gas and say, "We're just going to run at that because we know we can sell here. We know we win pretty much every time when we meet these conditions. Let's go do that."
turns.zh: 所以一旦你开始感觉「我在这有模式了，它开始聚焦」，那我觉得你准备好真收紧、把脚踩油门说「我们就冲那个，因为我们知道我们能在这卖。我们知道在这些条件下我们几乎每次都赢。去做」。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm really glad we touched on this topic. I mentioned to you earlier that I was at a meetup last night and I was talking about this podcast that I'm starting and I asked who they'd love to hear on this podcast, and your name was the first name this guy brought up. And so-
turns.zh: 我超高兴我们聊到这话题。我早跟你提过我昨晚在个 meetup，聊我正开始的这播客，我问他们想听谁上，你的名字是这人第一个提出的。所以——

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: That's awesome.
turns.zh: 那超棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... he's a huge fanboy. And I asked him what question he would ask you.
turns.zh: ——他是个大粉丝。我问他想问你啥问题。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: I have fans. That's so cool.
turns.zh: 我有粉丝。那太酷了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're out there. You're out there at meetups. And this is what he wanted to know actually is around just how do you think about this for startups and early stage stuff. So I'm glad we touched on it.
turns.zh: 你在那。你在 meetup 上。而他其实想知道的就是怎么为创业公司和早期想这个。所以我高兴我们聊到它。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The last topic I want to make sure we chat about, and this is what led to our conversation, we had a Twitter exchange about this was around segmentation versus personas and just how people confuse these things and how to think about these topics. And so I guess I'd love to get your take on just what's the difference between say segmentation and personas.
turns.zh: 我想确保聊的最后一个话题——这也是引我们对话的——我们在 Twitter 上就「细分」(segmentation) vs 「人物画像」(personas) 吵过，人们怎么混淆这些、怎么想这些话题。所以我想听你对细分和人物画像区别的看法。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Right. So you know how I said earlier marketers, we're really bad with definitions on things? And so everything in marketing is poorly defined and the marketers are always fighting over what do we mean when we say brand and things like this? So personas and segments, oh my gosh, terrible.
turns.zh: 对。所以你知道我前面说营销人我们对定义很糟？所以营销里一切都定义得差，营销人总为「我们说品牌时啥意思」打架。所以人物画像和细分，哦我的天，糟。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So now this I think stems from if you go to marketing school, a lot of what you learn in marketing school is very consumer oriented, like consumer product oriented. And so if you're selling to consumers, a lot of the ways a consumer market gets segmented ... So segmentation is the way you split up a market.
turns.zh: 这我觉来自：如果你去营销学校，你学的很多非常面向消费者、消费产品。所以如果你卖消费者，消费者市场细分的方式……细分是你切分市场的方式。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So the way you would segment a consumer market is you might say, "Well, I've got this toothpaste. And this toothpaste is for men under the age of 16 that want to get a date or something like that." And that would be how you would segment the market, which coincidentally sounds a lot like a persona.
turns.zh: 所以你会细分消费者市场说「嗯我有这牙膏。这牙膏给 16 岁以下想约到会的男的」之类。那会是你切分市场的方式，而它碰巧听起来很像人物画像。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So personas are about people and it's characteristics of a particular buyer, a particular type of buyer. And so we'll do personas to try to get really deep understanding of, who is this buyer? What are they care about? What are their hopes and dreams? What makes them scared? What makes them excited? What are they trying to get done? This kind of stuff.
turns.zh: 所以人物画像是关于人——一个特定买家的特征。我们做人物画像是为了深度理解：这买家是谁？他们在乎啥？他们的希望和梦想是啥？什么让他们怕？什么让他们兴奋？他们想搞定啥？这类事。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Now we go to B2B and that's not how we segment a market. We're not talking about 25 year old down to the age of whatever, whatever. We're segmenting the market on different things. And in fact, in B2B, we can segment a market on almost anything, but typically there would be what we call firmographics, like how big's the company? How many employees? How much revenue? What geography is it in? But then we often do segmentations on things that are nothing to do with that.
turns.zh: 现在我们到 B2B，那不是我们切分市场的方式。我们不是聊 25 岁到 whatever 岁。我们按不同的东西切分市场。事实上在 B2B，我们几乎能按任何东西切分，但典型会有我们叫「企业特征」(firmographics) 的东西——公司多大？多少员工？多少营收？在哪个地理？但然后我们常做跟那无关的切分。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So if we really want to target a set of customers, often we'll say, "You know what? My product is really good for folks that have a creative team with more than three people and a budget of this and they use this particular software package." We win all day, if we have that.
turns.zh: 所以如果我们真想打一组客户，常我们说「你知道吗？我的产品对『有超三人创意团队、有这预算、用这特定软件包』的人超好」。那种我们全天赢。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And that's a very actionable segmentation, I can go find companies that have that, I can make a list of companies that have that. And that's who my marketing and sales is going to go after. If sales needs to make a list of companies to go chase, that's that. And so in my mind, this is super important.
turns.zh: 那是超可执行的细分——我能去找有那个的公司、列个有那个的公司清单。那就是我的市场和销售要打的。如果销售要列公司清单去追，就那个。所以在我心里这超重要。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Coming back to the previous question, when we were talking about, I'm starting to see the patterns in who loves my stuff and why, I'm not talking about the person there, I'm talking about the kind of company. What is common amongst the companies that love us, that I can segment the market and say, "Look, if your company is this size, you have this software package, you have this and this," I'm going to win all day.
turns.zh: 回到前面的问题，我们聊「我开始看到谁爱我的东西、为啥的模式」——我不是在聊那的人，我聊的是那类公司。爱我们的公司之间有啥共同点，让我能切分市场说「看，如果你公司这规模、你有这软件包、你有这和这」，我全天赢。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so I need to understand that deeply in order to build my whole go-to market strategy, in order to have marketing campaigns that resonate with those kinds of companies, in order to make a list, if my sales are doing outbound, or if I'm doing target account selling, or ABM, how do I make that list of who I'm going after, that kind of stuff.
turns.zh: 所以我需要深度理解那个，才能建我的整个 GTM 策略、才能有跟那类公司 resonate 的市场活动、才能列清单——如果销售做 outbound、或我做目标客户销售、或 ABM——我怎么做那个我要打谁的清单，之类。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Then we have personas. Now again, if I'm selling a consumer thing, maybe all I care about is personas, all I care about is who's this person who's the buyer. B2B, everything's a little bit more complicated than that. So in a typical B2B purchase process, particularly if it's what we would call enterprise software, even if it's not very expensive enterprise software, typically we have between five and seven people are involved in what we call making the decision for what gets bought.
turns.zh: 然后我们有人物画像。again，如果我卖消费者东西，也许我只在乎人物画像，只在乎买家这人是谁。B2B 一切更复杂。典型 B2B 购买流程，尤其我们叫企业软件，即便不贵，通常有 5 到 7 个人参与「决定买啥」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So if I come back to my example earlier where the VP sales decides they need a CRM and they pick on poor John, and then John's got to go figure it out. John, that persona, let's say he's the sales ops manager, we would make a sales ops manager persona that would capture that person, but there's other people involved in this deal.
turns.zh: 所以回到我前面的例子：销售 VP 决定需要 CRM、挑了可怜的 John，然后 John 得搞定。John，那人物画像，假设他是销售运营经理，我们会做个销售运营经理的人物画像 capture 那人，但这单里还有别人。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So as part of figuring out which CRM to buy, when he got in the later stages of the deal, he probably consults some of the sales reps, because they're going to be the end users of this thing, and so he doesn't want to pick something that they're all going to hate.
turns.zh: 所以作为搞清楚买哪个 CRM 的一部分，到单子后期，他大概会咨询一些销售代表，因为他们是终端用户，所以他不想选个他们全恨的。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: He's probably got an IT department and IT probably gets to say about, well, does it meet our security and compliance stuff? And we're going to have to take care of it. Does it integrate with what we need to integrate with? Can it suck in data or push out data to our data warehouse or whatever? So that person has a say.
turns.zh: 他大概有 IT 部门，IT 大概会说什么——它满足我们的安全和合规吗？我们得照顾它。它能跟我们要整合的整合吗？它能吸数据或推数据到我们数据仓库或 whatever 吗？所以那人有发言权。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: There might be a purchasing department. There might be legal involved. There might be head of security involved. There might be chief security officers. Somebody gets their nose in there and gets involved in that. So five to seven people involved in this deal.
turns.zh: 可能有采购部门。可能有法务。可能有安全头。可能有 CISO。某人把鼻子伸进来参与。所以 5 到 7 个人参与这单。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so here's where I think we go off the rails in marketing. So what I see marketing teams doing is they'll do personas for all those people. So they'll have this sheet and the sheet will say, Eric, the IT person doesn't like talking on the phone, who really likes video games. And they'll have this stereotype of Eric, the IT person. And then they'll say, Janet, the sales rep really outgoing, loves talking to people on the phone. Doesn't know what a video game is, that sort of thing.
turns.zh: 所以这是我觉得营销跑偏的地方。我看到营销团队给那些人都做人物画像。所以他们有张表，表上说「Eric，IT 那人不喜欢打电话，超爱电子游戏」。他们有 Eric 的刻板印象。然后说「Janet，销售代表超外向，爱打电话。不知道电子游戏是啥」之类。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So for positioning work, I'm going to say something that is contentious, but I don't think it is at all. Think about how the deal gets done. Here's how this actually happens. Vice president says to John, "Go figure it out." John then does all this research and figures out how to get a short list.
turns.zh: 所以为了定位工作，我要说句有争议、但我觉的一点都不的话：想想单子怎么成的。实际发生的是：VP 对 John 说「去搞定」。John 然后做所有研究、搞清楚怎么做短名单。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And then John might actually go all the way through to having calls with sales people and all this sort of stuff with all the vendors. And then John's really getting down to, okay, I'm going to pick this thing over this thing and then starts bringing in the other people.
turns.zh: 然后 John 可能一路走到跟销售代表打电话、跟所有供应商搞这些事。然后 John 真在降到「我要选这个 over 那个」，然后开始把其他人带进来。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So by far the most important persona that matters is that one. We call this the champion in the account because this person, their job is to get consensus and champion the deal across everybody, including their boss, who's the actual economic buyer, the person that writes the check.
turns.zh: 所以目前为止最重要的那个人物画像就是那个。我们叫它账户里的 champion (champion in the account)，因为这人的工作是拿到共识、把单子跨过所有人 champion，包括他老板——真正的经济买家、写支票的人。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so if our positioning doesn't resonate for that champion, we're dead in the water. We don't even get on a short list. We don't even get to care about all the other personas, if we don't nail it with John because John's a gatekeeper.
turns.zh: 所以如果我们的定位不对那 champion resonate，我们 dead in the water。我们连短名单都进不了。我们连在乎其他人物画像的资格都没有，如果我们没用 John 钉死——因为 John 是守门人。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So my positioning needs to crush it with John. And at some point way down the road, I need to arm John to be able to sell IT, to be able to sell purchasing, to be able to make sure everybody is cool on the user side and to be able to sell their boss, who's the economic buyer.
turns.zh: 所以我的定位得 crush John。而在远一点的将来，我得武装 John 能去卖 IT、能去卖采购、能确保用户侧所有人都 cool、能去卖他老板（经济买家）。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And so I think there's really only one persona that really, really matters in this, which is the champion in the account. And we should be very thoughtful and we should really have our arms around that persona. And then later in the deal cycle, we need to figure out how to arm that persona to go sell to all the other constituents in the deal. But if we don't nail that champion persona, we got nothing.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得这真只有一个人物画像真、真重要，就是账户里的 champion。我们该非常深思、该真把臂弯围住那人物画像。然后在单子周期后期，我们得搞清楚怎么武装那人物画像去卖单子里所有其他干系人。但如果我们没钉死那 champion 人物画像，我们啥也没有。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So I think it is an utter waste of time for marketing to build these stupid little one pager persona things for these 17 million personas and treat them like they're the same as the champion, when the champion matters times a thousand and all we really need to do is figure out how to arm the champion, because the champion's going to do this, the heavy lifting of selling IT. We're likely not even going to get all that involved. Gee, that's my [inaudible 00:58:12].
turns.zh: 所以我觉得营销去建那些蠢的一页纸人物画像给那 1700 万个画像、把它们当得跟 champion 一样，是彻头彻尾的浪费时间——而 champion 重要一千倍，我们真正要做的只是搞清楚怎么武装 champion，因为 champion 会做卖 IT 的重活。我们可能根本不会那么参与。天，那是我的……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was amazing. I've never heard it described so directly and clearly. And so I think that's actually a good way to just wrap things up. I feel like I've sucked up enough of your time. Where can folks find your book, contact you if they want to work with you, anything like that?
turns.zh: 那超棒。我从没听过这么直接清楚地描述。所以我觉得那其实是收尾的好方式。我觉得我吸够你的时间了。人们能在哪找到你的书、联系你、想合作的话，这类？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Sure. The book's called Obviously Awesome, and you can Google me and find that wherever books are sold. And then there's an audio book, if that's your jam or an E-book or whatever. And then my website is aprildunford.com, so you can find me there. I'm on LinkedIn, I'm on Twitter. I'm @aprildunford on social media, but I don't really do any social media except Twitter and a little bit of LinkedIn these days because I'm feeling less certain about the future of Twitter, but yeah.
turns.zh: 行。书叫《Obviously Awesome》，你谷歌我、在任何卖书的地方都能找到。还有有声书、电子书之类。我的网站是 aprildunford.com，那能找到我。我在 LinkedIn、Twitter。社交媒体上我是 @aprildunford，但我除了 Twitter 和一点 LinkedIn 基本不用社交媒体了，因为我对 Twitter 的未来不太确定，但 yeah。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your tweets are great by the way. I highly recommend following April on Twitter.
turns.zh: 顺便，你的推文超棒。我强烈推荐关注 April 的 Twitter。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Oh good. Yeah, follow of me on Twitter.
turns.zh: 哦好。对，在 Twitter 上关注我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 听众能怎么帮到你？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: That's a great question. I don't know. Well, one thing I will say that I really love about Twitter is I use Twitter a lot to clarify my thinking on things. And so I really appreciate smart interactions with people on Twitter because sometimes I'll have a half-baked idea. And it's one of the things that I really like about Twitter versus LinkedIn, if I have a half-baked idea, I throw it out on LinkedIn and everyone goes, "That's great April," and that's it. Whereas if I have a half-baked idea and I throw it out on Twitter, people aren't shy about telling me I'm wrong.
turns.zh: 好问题。我不知道。嗯，一件事我超爱 Twitter 的是，我用 Twitter 很多去厘清我对事的思想。所以我真 appreciate 人们在 Twitter 上聪明的互动，因为有时我有个半生不熟的想法。Twitter vs LinkedIn 我更爱的一点是：如果我在 LinkedIn 抛个半生不熟的想法，每个人都「那超棒 April」，就那样。但如果我在 Twitter 抛个半生不熟的想法，人们不害羞告诉我我错了。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: And I appreciate it because I think that's how your thinking gets clearer. I mean, I'd like you to be nice about it if possible, but I like it when people jump in and they go, "Well, actually that doesn't really work if it's this, this and this." And you're like, "Ooh yeah, actually, you're right. Never really thought about that before."
turns.zh: 我 appreciate，因为我觉得那才是你的思想变清晰的方式。我的意思是，如果可能的话我希望你 nice 点，但我喜欢人们跳进来说「嗯其实如果是这、这、这，那不真工作」。你「哦对，其实你是对的。从没那么想过」。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So people that follow me on Twitter are really useful that way. And then I think I have this really engaged, thoughtful bunch of people following me on Twitter, people that are really interested in this stuff. And so I think it's kind of fun to be able to bat some deeper ideas around on stuff and not just have everybody go thumbs up, yay, April. That's kind of boring to me.
turns.zh: 所以关注我 Twitter 的人在那方面真有用。然后我觉得我有一群超投入、深思的人关注我 Twitter，真对这东西感兴趣的人。所以能抛些更深的点子来回打、而不只是每个人都点赞「yay April」，那挺好玩。那对我有点 boring。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Radical candor, that's what you need.
turns.zh: Radical candor，那是你需要的。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Oh yeah, I appreciate the thumbs up. Give me the thumbs up, but if that's all I was trying to do, then I wouldn't be throwing out as much half-baked, sort of controversial hot takes on Twitter as I do.
turns.zh: 哦对，我 appreciate 点赞。给我点赞，但如果那是我唯一想做的，那我不会在 Twitter 抛那么多半生不熟、有点争议的热门观点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I use Twitter in a very similar way, and so I completely understand that aspect.
turns.zh: 我用 Twitter 非常类似，所以我完全理解那方面。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Yeah, it's great for that.
turns.zh: 对，那对它超棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's amazing for that. April, thank you so much for making time. I learned a ton and I really appreciate your time.
turns.zh: 那对它超棒。April，太感谢你抽时间。我学到超多，真 appreciate 你的时间。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: All right. Well, thanks so much for having me and congratulations on the new podcast. I'm so excited for it.
turns.zh: 好。嗯，太感谢你邀请我，恭喜新播客。我超兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Me too. Me too. That was awesome. Thank you for listening. If you enjoyed the chat, don't forget to subscribe to the podcast. You could also learn more at lennyspodcast.com. I'll see you in the next episode.
turns.zh: 我也是。我也是。那超棒。感谢收听。如果你喜欢这聊天，别忘了订阅播客。你也能在 lennyspodcast.com 了解更多。下期见。
